title: Naming the core tradeoffs: latency vs throughput, performance vs scalability
why: Trains you to frame a design as competing forces you can articulate, not a single 'fast/good' knob.
explanation: The single most useful habit at this level is refusing to say 'fast.' Fast hides two different things. Latency is how long one request takes end to end: the user clicked and waited 300ms. Throughput is how many requests you finish per secon

title: Caching: what it buys and what it costs (staleness, invalidation)
why: Builds the reflex that a cache is a consistency tradeoff, not free speed — invalidation is where the real design decision lives.

title: Modeling an API around resources and HTTP verbs (Richardson levels 1-2)
why: Trains the difference between tunneling RPC over HTTP and designing addressable resources with honest verbs and status codes.
explanation: Most APIs that call themselves REST are really RPC wearing an HTTP costume. You can spot it fast: one endpoint, POST /api, and the real intent lives in a JSON body like {"action":"getUser","id":42}. That's Richardson Level 0 — HTTP as a dum

title: RDBMS vs NoSQL and normalization vs denormalization on purpose
why: Trains you to pick a store from access patterns and consistency needs rather than familiarity or hype.
explanation: Start from how the data is read and written, not from what you already run in prod. Relational databases earn their keep when you have entities with real relationships, ad-hoc queries you can't predict, and transactions that must be atomic

title: Read replicas and sharding: what they solve and what they break
why: Trains the judgment that replication buys reads at the cost of replication lag, and sharding buys scale at the cost of cross-shard joins and hot keys.
explanation: Read replicas solve one problem: too many reads for one primary. You copy writes from the primary to N replicas and send reads there. What you buy is read throughput and a warm standby. What you break is 'read-your-writes' — replication lag

title: Designing contracts that survive retries: idempotency and versioning
why: Trains you to treat 'the network will retry' as a given and design idempotent, evolvable interfaces instead of hoping calls happen once.

title: Bounded contexts: cutting systems along language and ownership seams
why: Trains you to decompose by model boundaries and human vocabulary rather than technical layers, which is what makes a split hold up.

title: CQRS: a scalpel for a few contexts, a trap for the whole system
why: Trains disciplined pattern selection — CQRS pays off only in complex or read/write-asymmetric contexts, and blindly applying it adds risk and kills productivity.

title: Consistency without distributed transactions: sagas, outbox, compensations
why: Trains you to accept that 2PC isn't an option across services and to design explicit compensating flows and atomic publish (outbox) instead of pretending ACID spans the fleet.

title: Failure as the default: the fallacies of distributed computing and resiliency patterns
why: Trains you to design assuming the network is unreliable and slow, so timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers are part of the design, not afterthoughts.
explanation: The fallacies of distributed computing are the lies every junior design tells itself: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology doesn't change, there's one admin, transport cost is zero

title: Sacrificial architecture: designing for ~10x growth and graceful replacement
why: Trains the long-horizon judgment that today's right architecture will be outgrown, so you invest in module boundaries that make future replacement cheap rather than chasing a forever-design.

title: Leading design review: making others' designs better without being right
why: Trains the Staff skill of surfacing risk and alternatives in a design doc/RFC while creating space for the author, instead of imposing your preferred answer.

why: Trains the socio-technical judgment that you ship your org chart, so architecture and team topology must be designed as one decision.
